The answer is: (a Canadian Indian reserve in British Columbia) went to the town of Fort St. James to hunt down the men who had killed one of their children. The Fort St. James Assessment Roll for 1924–25 contains an entry concerning the event: "Two men from Egulac came to Fort St. James to hunt down the men who had killed one of their children. They arrived in Fort St. James on September 23, 1924, and stayed at the home of Mr. Xavier Charles Mercier, fortifying and provisioning themselves while they waited for the desired quarry to appear. On September 27, the Egulac men left Fort St. James, one going north and the other south. The one who went north reached a mountain pass on the evening of October 4 and there encountered the party of four men he had been seeking. A fight ensued, during which both sides suffered losses, but in which the Egulac man was finally subdued and arrested. The party of four consisted of three whites and one half-caste, and they were camped peacefully at the pass, waiting for the game to come to them. The Egulac man, whose name is given as John Isaac, was taken to Fort St. James, where he was placed in custody by the North West Mounted Police. Isaac was sentenced to twelve months in jail for his part in the fight, and was paroled in March 1925. The roll then notes that "This Indian was released from prison on March 21, 1925, and returned to his home at Egulac."

Source: "Fort St. James Assessment Roll, 1924–1925" (PDF). British Columbia Archives. Government Publishers. 1925. pp. 13–14.

The answer is: (a Canadian Indian reserve in British Columbia) went to the town of Fort St. James to hunt down the men who had killed one of their children. The other child was spared because she was married to a white man. The two men were arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and taken to Fort St. James where they were put on trial for murder. The trial was held in St. James Hall on October 18, 1918. The courtroom was packed with Indians from nearby reserves who had been brought in by bus. The two men were found guilty and sentenced to hang. The case was appealed to the British Columbia Supreme Court in Vancouver. The appeal was heard by Chief Justice M. D. Macdonald. He set aside the verdict and sentence of the Fort St. James court and ordered a new trial. At the new trial the two men were again found guilty of murder and sentenced to hang. The case was appealed to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. The appeal was heard on December 15, 1919. The decision of the Privy Council was released on October 12, 1920. It was ruled that the Fort St. James court had been correct in finding the men guilty of murder, but that they had been sentenced to hang without due consideration of the circumstances of the crime. The men were resentenced to death by hanging, but this sentence was never carried out because of the general amnesty for criminals during World War I. The two men were released from prison in 1921.

When she opened the door, she was confronted by two men, one of whom pointed a pistol at her and demanded that she accompany them. She refused and attempted to reach for her own pistol, whereupon she was clubbed in the head and dragged out of her house. As she was being led down the street, she managed to free herself from her captors and run back to her house, where she managed to get off a shot in the dark at one of them, hitting him in the face. History
In 1913, Charles Mercier had moved from Fort St. James to Egulac, where he married a woman of the tribe. Some years later he left the tribe and returned to Fort St. James, where he operated a successful farm. In 1924, a man from the tribe shot and killed one of Mercier's sons. The two men responsible were arrested and held in jail at Fort St. James until they could be tried. The trial was to take place in December 1924. The two men from Egulac arrived in Fort St. James in October 1924 to wait and see how the trial would unfold. They stayed at the home of Xavier Charles Mercier, who was not related to the man whose son had been killed.In November 1924, the two men from Egulac left Fort St. James. But one of the two young men had seen the Chief of the Harbour and now he was very afraid. "Why are you afraid?" said the Chief of the Harbour. "I am the Chief of the Harbour and I save people from the water." "Then why did you come to our village?" "I came to your village to marry one of your daughters." At this the young men laughed. "You are old," they said. "You are the Chief of the Harbour and you are old." The Chief of the Harbour went away laughing to himself. And that is the story of the Chief of the Harbour. (From "Ravine," by Thomas King.) What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: It is a story about the power of fear and the importance of understanding the world around us. The Chief of the Harbour, who is really the ruler of the sea, could have punished the young men for their fear, but instead he chose to laugh at their ignorance. By not understanding the true nature of the world, the young men were left in fear, but with the help of the Chief of the Harbour, they were able to overcome that fear.

They escaped to the shore, and hid behind a log. Now canoes came up, and they heard the noise of paddles, and saw one canoe coming up to them. The people came down to the water and they began to fight, and many were killed. But presently the young man heard one of the warriors say, "Quick, let us go home: that man has been hit." Now he thought: "Oh, they are ghosts." He did not feel sick, but they said he had been shot. So the canoes went back to Egulac and the young man went ashore to his house and made a fire. And he told everybody and said: "Behold I accompanied the ghosts, and we went to fight. Many of our fellows were killed, and many of those who attacked us were killed. They said I was hit, and I did not feel sick." He told it all, and then he became quiet. When the sun rose he fell down. Something black came out of his mouth. His face was contorted. The people jumped up and cried. He was dead.

"Arrows are in the canoe," they said. "I will count how many there are." When they had counted them he said, "There are five arrows." "Good!" they said. "Sometimes we shoot one, and sometimes we shoot two." But, just as they were going to start, there came a loud noise behind them, and they said, "Wow! How scary! That must have been a bear!" One of the young men said, "I will go and get some sticks." When he had got some sticks he gave one arrow to each of the others, and they began to shoot.
They had not shot a single arrow when a voice came from the canoe, "Why do you shoot arrows at night?" "We thought it was a war-party," they said. "Where are the war-parties?" "They have gone to the sandbars." "But we are not war-parties; we are canoes full of young men." "Sometimes war-parties come in canoes." "That may be so," they said, "but we are not war-parties." "What is the difference between war-parties and not war-parties?" "The difference is that war-parties shoot arrows in the daytime, and not at night." "
